Marsh & McLennan Cos. is urging US regulators to allow banks to hold less capital against loans covered by credit risk insurance as they look for new ways to offload data center exposure.
Demand for hedging AI-related finance has exploded, but US lenders have traditionally leaned more heavily on other instruments because insurance doesn’t free up regulatory capital for them, according Azi Larsen, a managing director in the credit specialties practice at the world’s biggest insurance broker.
“We’ve been doing a lot of advocacy around that in the US,” Larsen said in an interview with Bloomberg News. “Hopefully we’ll have a positive answer from the US regulators at the end of the year,” she added.
The Federal Reserve is set to complete its latest regulatory capital rules in the coming weeks, Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said at an event on Nov 10. The package is expected to include a plan that would lower the capital surcharge for the biggest US lenders and another that would change risk-based capital requirements for midsize and large banks.
Credit risk insurance has long been used by European banks to mitigate losses and release capital that can then be used to issue more loans. Lenders pay premiums to cover a percentage of losses on specific facilities. Barclays Plc has been looking to buy cover on more than $10 billion of data center debt, while HSBC Holdings Plc has explored a similar transaction.
With global spending on data centers projected by McKinsey & Co to hit $6.7 trillion by 2030, debt financing is expected to play a much bigger role, and finding different tools to manage risks has become “mission critical” for lenders, Larsen said.
Marsh is active in arranging credit risk insurance for project finance, including deals related to data centers. Despite its limitations, US lenders are increasingly turning to the product to cap their exposure to certain borrowers or industries as the volume of AI-related lending balloons.
“Even if they don’t get capital relief, they still see value in trying to use it,” Larsen added.

SpaceX must face a lawsuit accusing it of illegally firing eight engineers who raised concerns about alleged sexual harassment and discrimination at the company after a US appeals court on Tuesday rejected its request to send the case to private arbitration.
The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a federal judge’s ruling that the engineers’ claims were exempt from the arbitration agreements they signed at SpaceX and can continue in court.
Spokespeople for SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the decision. SpaceX has denied the allegations.
The engineers’ attorney, Laurie Burgess, said they were “delighted” with the court’s “well-reasoned” decision. The engineers filed the lawsuit in 2024, claiming SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordered their firing after they circulated a letter calling the billionaire a “distraction and embarrassment” and urging executives to disavow sexually charged comments he made on social media.
The lawsuit said Musk’s conduct fostered a “pervasively sexist culture” at SpaceX where female engineers were routinely subjected to harassment and sexist comments.
The 9th Circuit on Tuesday rejected SpaceX’s argument that the claims were not covered by a federal law that allows individuals to pursue lawsuits in “sexual harassment disputes” regardless of arbitration agreements.

Five US states have joined the Federal Trade Commission in a lawsuit that alleges telehealth company Hims & Hers Health engaged in deceptive and unlawful privacy practices, the FTC said on Oct. 10.
The lawsuit alleges the company shared consumers’ sensitive health information with third-party advertising platforms including Meta Platforms and Snap, despite claiming its services maintain consumers’ privacy.
The case also contends Hims & Hers deceives users about its billing and cancellation practices, according to the FTC.
The amended complaint filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California now includes Arizona, Florida, Nebraska, Ohio and Wisconsin and alleges violations of the states’ consumer protection laws in addition to federal laws, the FTC said in a statement.
Los Angeles County and Utah joined the action when the FTC initiated it in July.
Hims & Hers is one of the largest telehealth players in the market for weight-loss drugs. It also treats erectile dysfunction, hair loss and mental health conditions, shipping prescriptions directly to customers.
“We will vigorously defend ourselves against these follow-on claims, which rely on the same flawed allegations advanced in the government’s lawsuit,” a Hims & Hers spokesperson said.
The FTC alleged Hims & Hers charges users for prescription drugs before they meet with healthcare providers and makes it difficult to cancel subscriptions.
The company cut its full-year core profit forecast on Monday as higher costs tied to a pivot to branded weight-loss drugs and international expansion pressured margins.

In October, Shell Plc held a “DE&I in Action and World Mental Health” day, focused on inclusion and mental wellbeing. Staff in the US and elsewhere were encouraged to reflect on their experiences at work, to “practice care, courage and curiosity” and to use a special video-conference background to mark the occasion.
For an oil major that does business with the US government, the mere existence of the event is notable.
At a time when many global companies are downplaying diversity measures, London-headquartered Shell — which counts the US as its biggest country market — is vocal in its commitment to diversity, equity and inclusion, calling it “a key driver for our winning performance culture.” That stance helps Shell comply with global diversity regulations that are non-negotiable for businesses based outside of the US. But it also increases the risk of scrutiny from the Trump administration and conservative activists.
Shell’s DEI commitment has become central to legal challenges filed by three current or former employees represented by an activist group co-founded by President Donald Trump’s new Chief of Staff, Stephen Miller. The workers claim to have been discriminated against because they are White, describing a team restructure that favored ethnic-minority colleagues and foreign nationals, as well as a manager who they say gave them “tear jars” as jokey leaving gifts, which they found insensitive.

Employment discrimination lawsuits don’t typically threaten large corporations’ core operations or business viability. And people with knowledge of the oil and gas sector said that firms like Shell broadly have good relationships with the Trump administration and more pressing concerns than DEI.

Tech companies WiseTech and Atlassian have cut jobs this year, attributing the losses to AI. Telecommunications firm Telstra has also cut jobs from an AI joint venture with Accenture, with some work offshored to India.
More broadly, other firms across corporate Australia have also slashed their domestic headcounts while expanding operations in India, the Philippines and Vietnam, though they did not explicitly mention AI in their announcements.
When asked about the Qantas job cuts, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who was unveiling the response to a recent breach of a government website by an OpenAI agent, said AI “represents an enormous opportunity and a major economic issue.”
Labour unions have argued that Australian workers were not being replaced by AI, but by lower-paid offshore employees.

“From Qantas to the big banks, workers deserve transparency and genuine consultation over decisions that impact their jobs and lives.”
The Australian Services Union, which represents the affected Qantas workers, accused the airline of “using AI to launder their cuts to Australian jobs.”

A New York City sightseeing helicopter on a maintenance flight made an emergency landing on Tuesday at a New Jersey cargo port after the pilot reported possible engine trouble.
Two people were aboard the Bell 206L-4 helicopter when it came down on a road at the Port Jersey Marine Terminal in Bayonne, across the Hudson River from Manhattan, around 8:55 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration said.
No injuries were reported, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said. Messages seeking comment were left for the helicopter’s operator, FlyNYON.
Video of the scene shows part of the helicopter’s tail sitting on the road about 30 feet (9 meters) from the aircraft, which was manufactured in 1999, according to FAA records.
In a recording of the air traffic control audio posted on the ATC app, the pilot can be heard saying, “Mayday, mayday, mayday” and “We need to land outside of the airport.” The helicopter landed several minutes later, just outside of the container terminal, the Port Authority said.
Last year, a Bell 206L-4 sightseeing helicopter plummeted into the Hudson River, killing all 6 people on board. The National Transportation Safety Board said the remains of several geese were found on the helicopter, suggesting it may have struck several birds before crashing.
NYC Helicopter Crash Prompts Push for New Tourist-Flight Rules
Last week, the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Office of Inspector General announced an audit of sightseeing helicopter regulations, citing “longstanding concerns regarding the industry’s safety and whether the current regulatory framework provides adequate safeguards.”
Since 2008, there have been at least 58 helicopter crashes involving tourist helicopters in the U.S., including 11 that were fatal, Assistant Inspector General Marshall Jackson said.

The tally of losses from the historic wildfires in Washington over the summer continues to grow, but by so do the lessons being learned.
Insured losses from the wildfires that plagued Washington for nearly half the summer are nearing $1 billion from roughly 3,500 claims, far exceeding projections of $600 million in September for what has become the most expensive wildfires in state history.
Those figures encompass all wildfires in the state from June to present, but most losses are from the Spokane Complex Fire, comprised of the Old Trails, Fairview and Autumn Lane fires that destroyed roughly 900 structures. An analysis from property data provider Cotality identified 5,256 properties that sustained at least some damage, of which 96% were single-family residences.
The fires, which ignited on Aug. 1, grew to 10,000-acres-plus, burned 19 days and prompted evacuations of more than 65,000 people.
The biggest insured loss came from the Old Trails Fire, which occurred in the wildland-urban interface, with an estimated $665 million in insured losses.
The blaze was studied by the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety researchers, who looked into how factors such as structure spacing, connective fuels and building components interact under the fire weather conditions.
The IBHS research on the Old Trails Fire in Spokane County, which destroyed 615 structures, shows connective fuels like combustible fences and mulch created pathways for fire to reach homes.
Researchers documented damage and fire-spread pathways at 132 structures across nine areas, identifying vulnerabilities involving windows, decks, building materials and other structural features.
Aerial imagery captured just six hours after ignition showed multiple fire outbreaks burning simultaneously. That stretched firefighting resources and left crews unable to protect all the threatened structures, according to the report.
“As a result, structures with vulnerabilities to ember exposure, including combustible roofs, unmitigated vents, or fuels directly adjacent to the home, remain(ed) at risk of ignition,” the IBHS report states. “This scenario led to significant losses within the perimeter, even after the advancing fire front had slowed, and illustrates the challenges of structure protection, fire suppression, and fire management in communities with vulnerable structures.”
Researchers looked at the January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires to compare the distances between the structures in the Eaton Fire with structural distances in the Old Trails Fire. They concluded the Washington fire could have been worse had the housing density been greater.
They found that most (58%) structures in the Eaton Fire had another structure within 10 feet, while only 13.8% of structures within the Old Trails Fire perimeter were spaced so closely.
Fire-resistant building materials alone were not always enough to keep a home safe. Researchers identified instances in which combustible landscaping allowed flames to reach fire-resistant exterior walls.
In one case, burning mulch ignited combustible components beneath noncombustible lap siding where a wall met the foundation. Another exposure involving a stone-veneer wall did not result in an ignition, possibly because flashing at the base of the wall helped protect combustible materials underneath, according to the report.

Reported ties between Jensen Huang, the CEO of AI powerhouse Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy have sparked an investigation by the FBI, calls for congressional hearings, a review by the company’s independent directors and a proposed investor class action lawsuit.
Below is a look at the potential legal exposure for Huang, Nvidia NVDA.O and the directors of the company, which dominates the global market for computer chips that power the AI economy.
WHAT ARE THE ALLEGATIONS?
The New York Times reported last month that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, whom US authorities investigated and concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. Megaspeed has faced US scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Beijing gain access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips whose export to China is restricted.
On Sunday, Nvidia’s Huang admitted he was unfaithful to his wife without providing details about the relationship, which led to a drop in Nvidia’s stock price. Trump said Huang told him that he had no idea that the woman was a spy and Huang has not been accused of criminal wrongdoing.
Reuters could not independently verify the intelligence allegation, which China’s foreign ministry has said was “groundless,” nor has it verified Alice Huang’s current employment status with Megaspeed.
Nvidia has said its board has “no reason to believe” US national security or company secrets were affected, though an independent committee of directors will review all available information. The company said on Tuesday the independent directors hired the Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz law firm to assist with its investigation.
Nvidia sits at the center of the technological rivalry between the United States and China. Washington has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China since 2022. News of the affair has emerged as Democrats seized control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, propelled in part by anti-AI and anti-corruption sentiment.
WHAT ABOUT FEDERAL SECURITIES FRAUD?
A proposed class action was filed in San Jose, California, federal court on Monday alleging the company and Huang defrauded shareholders by concealing Huang’s alleged relationship. The proposed class would cover Nvidia investors who bought the stock between October 9, when Nvidia denied claims in a New York Times report about Megaspeed ties to China, and November 8, when the board announced its investigation and Huang acknowledged he had an affair. The period includes October 30, when Huang told Bloomberg Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed was “normal and not unusual.”
Securities fraud plaintiffs must show, among other things, that Nvidia and Huang knowingly misled investors, that investors relied on those misleading statements and that those misleading statements artificially inflated the stock.
The lawsuit did not specify damages but the stock lost around 20% during the class period, a decline of around $1 trillion in market value.
Such lawsuits are often filed in the wake of a company’s stock suffering a large drop, and more are likely.

The U.K. economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, in line with estimates, driven by output in the services sector.
Economists polled by Reuters had expected the economy to grow 0.7% from the previous quarter.
The economy grew 1.9% year-on-year in the three months to September.
The figures showed a slight improvement from the previous quarter, when gross domestic product grew by 0.5%. In the first quarter, the economy grew by 0.6%.
Services sector growth
The services sector expanded by 0.9%, data from the U.K.'s Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed on Thursday morning. It offset 0.1% output growth in the production sector and a 0.7% contraction in construction.
Within the services sector, information and communication was a key driver of growth, expanding by 2.1% in the quarter.
"This industry has been the largest driver of GDP growth across 2026, with evidence that many of the businesses reporting the largest increases in turnover are involved in activities related to artificial intelligence and cloud computing," the ONS said.
"However, because of the nature of our data collection, it is difficult for us to quantify the exact impact of these types of activities on turnover."
In September, the economy grew by 0.2% month-on-month, beating expectations that GDP would flatline. It marked an improvement from the previous month, with revised figures showing the British economy carved out zero growth in August.
U.K. finance minister John Healey said in a statement that the country was showing "stand-out resilience" despite the U.S.-Iran war hitting growth worldwide.
"Our U.K. economy is growing at the fastest rate in almost ten years, outside the pandemic," he said.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the third-quarter growth was "bringing hope for the future."
The British pound was down by 0.2% against the U.S. dollar and flat against the euro on Thursday morning. Yields on U.K. government bonds were little changed.
Scott Gardner, investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Personal Investing, called the update a "decent set of results with the UK economy still proving to be relatively resilient since the US-Iran war started."
But he added that the economy's strength will be tested in the months ahead.
"Nervousness in the lead up to the Autumn Budget and continued uncertainty from the Middle East war is expected to weigh on confidence and activity over the coming GDP readings," he said in a note.
"With some already trimming their growth forecasts for next year, the U.K. economy still faces several headwinds."
AI provides 'an extra engine of growth'
Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, said it had been "a strikingly strong third quarter" for the U.K.

Following a scorching start to his Major League career in 2023, the heralded Cardinals prospect slumped over the next two seasons.
Then it happened: Walker broke out with a performance commensurate with the lofty expectations. The 24-year-old right fielder hit 29 home runs, drove in 102 runs and stole 22 bases for St. Louis this past season, earning his first career All-Star selection. He even won the Home Run Derby in Philadelphia along the way, defeating heavyweight hometown favorite Kyle Schwarber.

The results were the fruit of a simplified approach he worked on with his hitting coaches during the offseason.
Defensively, Walker’s arm was one of the best among outfielders -- his average arm strength of 96.5 mph ranked in the 99th percentile, according to Statcast.

The New World screwworm has made a comeback in the US after months of relatively muted cases, thanks in large part to milder temperatures and humidity that are encouraging the deadly livestock parasite’s activity.
More than 40 cases of screwworm have been confirmed so far in November, already making it the worst month since the pest first appeared in Texas earlier this year, according to the US Department of Agriculture. Cases began accelerating in October, when the pest spread to Arizona for the first time.
There have been a total of nearly 130 cases in the US, with more than 60 currently active.
When screwworm first arrived in the US in June, “a lot of us were like, ‘Okay, yep, we’re in for a rough summer,'” said Caleb Hubbard, an assistant professor of urban entomology at New Mexico State University. But there were much fewer cases than feared.
In hindsight, the US had just gotten lucky: Screwworm flies like warm weather, but not the extreme above-100F days that Texas and New Mexico faced in July and August. The parasite is less active in such temperatures, both in movement and in reproduction. Colder temperatures — below 59F — also make the flies more sluggish.
“It was something that I think we all were like, ‘Whew, we got through it, we’re all good,'” Hubbard said of the hotter summer days. “But as temperatures have started to decline, at least in the Southwest, we’re kind of in this Goldilocks zone right now” for the screwworm.
The parasite’s life cycle can be as short as two to three weeks in ideal conditions, above 80F — but below 100F — with high humidity, according to Texas A&M University. Screwworms only mate once, but during that short window in that temperature zone they are more active, with greater opportunities for the population to grow.
Extreme heat in Texas when the fly first arrived created “actually a pretty hostile environment,” said Phillip Kaufman, an entomology professor at Texas A&M. “We finally have started getting some cooler weather — not cold, but cooler weather here, and there has been an uptick in rain events, particularly over Arizona, New Mexico, and West Texas,” exactly where the fly has been detected.
The spread to Arizona is “part of a natural progression” as the pest pushes westward from Texas, and northward from Mexico, Mykaela Martin, public information officer for the Arizona Department of Agriculture, said in an email.
Despite the rapid acceleration, the outbreak is still minuscule compared to the 95,000 cases that the US reckoned with in its worst outbreak in 1972. Cases at that time stretched across all of Texas, up into Oklahoma and as far west as California.
The USDA to a large degree was able to contain the current outbreak through the summer with livestock movement controls, a monitoring and surveillance program, and the dispersing of sterile flies for curbing the screwworm’s reproduction.
The agency said in an emailed statement that the current weather patterns are “certainly conditions that could cause an increase in fly survivability, though it is difficult to determine a sole reason” for the recent jump in cases.
Other explanations for the uptick in infections and wild flies caught in the USDA’s traps include the movement of animals. The fly does not travel very far on its own and depends on either livestock or wildlife to spread.

Tennessee regulators are warning about a growing “memo of sale” scam that can cost homeowners dearly and can complicate title and property insurance purchases.
The Tennessee Department of Commerce and Insurance, the state attorney general and others posted a bulletin this week that explained that, when sellers list their homes for sale, scammers may offer cash purchases. But instead of cash, the scammers will file a memorandum of sale with the clerk of court.
The memo notifies any other possible buyers about the pending sale and can prevent the homeowner from selling to another potential buyer, TDCI said in the bulletin. The scam company usually refuses to close on the sale, then demands a ransom of tens of thousands of dollars to clear the title.
“The homeowner is left with little recourse,” the department noted.
The scammers may claim to be real-estate wholesalers. But Tennessee regulations require that wholesalers must make “clear and conspicuous” disclosure of their intent to find third-party buyers, TDCI said.
The officials offered some words of advice for sellers:
- Pay attention to whether the sales contract contains language about recording a memorandum. Consider negotiating language that details when the memorandum will be removed.
- Ask clearly if the buyer intends to wholesale the property.
- Get everything in writing.
- Use TDCI’s Public Search to check the license status of the individual approaching the seller.
- If the buyer is demanding payment to release a memo, consult a licensed Tennessee attorney for guidance.
- File a complaint with the state Attorney General’s Office, Consumer Affairs Division
The department did not say how many sellers have been targeted by the scam.

Wall Street’s initial optimism following Tuesday’s midterm elections quickly turned into a sharp selloff, driven largely by concerns about the future of AI and data-center investments. But beyond the market’s volatility, the election results sent a message that leaders in Washington and Jefferson City should take seriously: Americans want relief from rising costs and a more stable future.
Democrats made major gains in Congress as many people voiced frustration about the cost of living, economic uncertainty, and national and foreign policies. Missouri’s results also showed a changing political landscape. Democrats gained seats in the state legislature, while Republicans lost their supermajorities in Jefferson City.
These results should not be seen only as a win for one party or a sign of political gridlock. They offer a chance to rethink policies that affect Missouri’s workers, farmers, families, and businesses. And the economic concerns behind that opportunity are real, not speculative.
Months before the election, an August 2026 Saint Louis University/YouGov survey of 900 likely Missouri voters documented widespread financial anxiety. 69% worried about affording health care, 66% about groceries and gasoline, 62% about utility bills, and 59% about property taxes. Only 25% rated Missouri’s economy as good or excellent, while just 21% gave the national economy similarly positive marks. The same survey found that 68% opposed construction of a new data center in their community.
The war with Iran added to economic pressures. As I discussed in my March analysis and June follow-up, the conflict’s effects on energy markets, transportation costs, and economic uncertainty extend well beyond the Middle East, reaching Missouri families, farmers, and businesses. Those economic consequences have since become part of the broader political debate, with even administration officials acknowledging the war’s role in the midterm backlash.
These findings do not establish why every Missourian voted as they did. But they show that economic dissatisfaction and concerns about the costs of technological development were already widespread before Election Day. The challenge now is to translate the demand for change into policies that deliver meaningful economic improvements.
Tariffs: An opportunity to reconsider the costs
Few policies show the gap between promises and reality as clearly as tariffs. You bought State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLE) to own the energy sector. On a $300,000 position, $116,286 of that money sits in just two oil companies. That is the hidden cost: diversification you think you own but may not.
Two Companies Hold Nearly 39 Cents of Every Dollar
XLE’s SEC Form N-PORT filing as of June 30, 2026 shows Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM | XOM Price Prediction) at 22.67% of net assets and Chevron (NYSE:CVX) at 16.09%. Together they make up 38.76% of the fund. On a $300,000 stake, that works out to $68,015 in Exxon and $48,271 in Chevron.
The drop-off after them is steep. The third-largest holding, ConocoPhillips (NYSE:COP), weighs in at 6.57%, or about $19,701 of the same position. Weights shift as prices move and the fund rebalances, so check XLE’s current holdings before acting on these figures.
A Low Fee Masks a Heavy Two-Stock Tilt
XLE’s expense ratio (shown as a share of assets) is 0.08%, per State Street’s fact sheet. That costs $8 per year per $10,000 invested, or $240 a year on $300,000. Few sector funds charge less. The larger cost here comes from portfolio construction.
Why a Sector Fund Ends Up Top-Heavy
XLE tracks the Energy Select Sector Index, which represents the energy companies inside the S&P 500. The index uses market-cap weighting, meaning each company’s slice depends on its total stock market value, and Exxon and Chevron are the biggest energy companies by that measure, so they get the biggest slices. On its fiscal Q3 2025 call, management described CTV, its connected-TV advertising, as its largest and fastest-growing channel. The company now emphasizes something else. So what is it?

Management now pitches AI agents that set up and fine-tune ad campaigns, citing internal figures that show better results for advertisers. AI itself is not new for management: in February 2026 it said it would discuss an agentic AI framework for partners, and in August 2026 it said it had added “tons of AI capabilities.” What has changed is CTV. In August 2026, on the fiscal Q2 2026 call, management cited over 50% CTV growth in both EMEA and APAC. The company still discusses CTV. Management listed it alongside agentic AI and measurement among its highest return opportunities on the latest call, but executives no longer highlight CTV’s growth.

A few months later, I got the opportunity to run the New York City Marathon. I was hesitant to accept, because I didn’t think I could run that far, but a few of my colleagues pushed me to say yes and really believed in me. So I signed up.

Jeremy Hurtt woke up that winter morning in 2014, and after staring at the ceiling for a few minutes, headed out for a run, thinking it may be his last.
He headed toward the spot where the run—and everything else—could end. An overpass above an interstate in the town of Benton, Arkansas, a mile from the house he had been crashing in for the past few weeks, sleeping on a cold floor, getting by on the generosity of a friend. Money had troubled Jeremy for years. He did odd jobs around town for a few bucks, but mostly was bumming $10 and $20 from friends just to get by. He was 34 years old, with nothing in the bank, no home, no car, not even a driver’s license. All these little indignities, piling up, had started to bury him.
And then there were the memories, too.
Since finishing a deployment in Iraq in 2008, there’d been lots of days when Jeremy felt down, depressed—and seemed different from the playful, clownish, upbeat guy his Army pals and others had come to know. “He was no longer good-time Jeremy,” one friend says. “He was withdrawn, reclusive.” But he never seriously thought about hurting himself. Until that morning when the indignities were too many, and his mind couldn’t stop wondering why he was still alive and better people weren’t.
The overpass was a destination he had crossed before. On walks and runs when he was up for it. At that early-morning hour, semitrucks would be rushing below. He, on the other hand, wasn’t rushing, running at his usual 8-to-9-minute pace, which let his mind race ahead. Running was something he had done occasionally, a means to an end after his return home from Iraq, a way to stay somewhat fit. That morning, running was the means to get where he needed to go.
He thought of what would happen if he decided to jump. About the driver whose vehicle would likely strike him once he landed on the road. He didn’t want to cause another person pain. He knew from his time in Iraq the pain that comes with sudden death. But even this good intention couldn’t deter him from running ahead.
He gave little thought to what might happen if he didn’t jump.

The change follows a deep selloff. Semiconductor shares trade about 38% below their June highs, and the multiples investors pay for them have compressed. At current prices, the analysts said, valuations imply earnings growth of only about 8% a year.

Politics Adds a New Worry to the AI Spending Debate
Democratic wins in the midterm elections, including in states that oppose new data centers, fueled concerns about regulation. A stricter permitting climate could slow construction and raise its cost, which would cut into the spending that has fed AI company revenue.

Why 2028 Worries Analysts More Than 2027
AI spending added about 8 percentage points to S&P 500 earnings growth over the past year. The Wells Fargo analysts wrote that "The tailwind is expected to continue in 2027," and that it largely disappears in 2028 as spending growth slows and depreciation costs rise.
Depreciation explains much of the concern. Companies spread the cost of data centers and chips over several years, so those charges keep landing on income statements even after the buying slows. Those charges are real expenses even though the cash left the company earlier. Profit growth then shrinks, just as the spending that lifted it fades. Analysts build their forecasts from spending levels, so a plateau in budgets changes the math quickly.
The bigger risk, the analysts said, is a downturn in earnings per share once capital spending peaks. They also pointed to extra supply arriving in 2028 that prices do not yet reflect. For investors, the question is how much of that is already in share prices after the drop.

The case for Procter & Gamble
Procter & Gamble operates as a global leader in consumer packaged goods, selling trusted brands across categories like beauty, grooming, and home care. A significant portion of its sales comes from mass merchandisers, and Walmart (WMT +0.41%) accounts for nearly 16% of total net sales. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, especially since the top ten customers represent roughly 43% of its sales.
Financial performance remained steady in FY 2026, with revenue reaching approximately $87.0 billion, a 3.3% increase over the previous year. As of its June 2026 balance sheet, the company reported a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.6x. The company is currently implementing its "Back to Starbucks" strategy to revitalize store experiences and improve operational efficiency. A group of nonprofits sued OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX’s AI division, Meta Platforms and Alphabet’s Google on Thursday, seeking to block the further development of the most advanced AI models over concerns, voiced by the companies’ own leaders, that the technology could pose a threat to humanity.
The nonprofits, which focus on tech accountability and include the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and Heat Initiative, sued in San Francisco, saying California’s laws against unfair business practices provide the grounds for a court order barring the companies from further development of products like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude.
The lawsuit cites comments from company leaders, like Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, and Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive, about AI’s potential to cause the destruction of civilization. It also describes recent incidents where models have escaped testing environments and autonomously attacked government websites.
“No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products—much less ones that could kill us all—as inevitable,” the lawsuit says. “Nor is any industry granted the right to self-regulate the development of such dangerous products.”
The lawsuit accuses the companies of engaging in business practices that create a public nuisance, or harm to public health and enjoyment, pointing to both past incidents and the potential for future harm.
A spokesperson for Meta declined to comment. Representatives of the other companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
OTHER LAWSUITS SEEK TO BAR DEVELOPMENT
While the Trump administration has so far declined to pursue large-scale AI regulation over fears it could harm the country’s ability to compete with China, states and private entities have sought to use lawsuits to force the companies to make changes.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI in June, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, saying it has harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users. In September, Florida asked the judge overseeing the lawsuit to bar OpenAI from developing new artificial intelligence models without outside oversight. That motion remains pending, according to court records.
After Florida’s filing, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company had paused training its most capable models and would not resume until they have additional safeguards in place.
“Governments have an important role to play in setting robust safety standards for AI, and we’re committed to working with Florida and other states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry – not just one company,” Pusateri said.
Separately, a group of eight states sued OpenAI last month in courts across the country alleging ChatGPT has coached its users — including teenagers — to harm themselves or others. OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment after the filing.
The states’ lawsuits seek financial penalties, as well as an order barring the company from developing self-improving AI models unless it can ensure those models are aligned with human values.

Billion-dollar wildfires in the US have become more than five times as frequent and 10 times as costly over the past two decades, according to a new analysis of the nation’s most destructive fires.
The analysis, from Climate Central, a nonprofit climate research and communications group, looks at individual fires each causing at least $1 billion in damage. Earlier federal estimates combined losses from many fires that occurred during the same wildfire season into a single disaster.
Thirty-one individual wildfires have crossed the $1 billion threshold since 1980, together costing nearly $186 billion and destroying more than 79,500 structures, the analysis finds. An estimated 373 people died in the fires.
The surge reflects both a changing climate and communities’ choices about development, said Adam Smith, the scientist who led the project. “Either way you look at it, the rise in damages relates to human activities,” he said.
From 2007 through 2026, the US experienced 26 billion-dollar wildfires, compared with five during the previous 20 years. Inflation-adjusted losses jumped to $170 billion from $15.6 billion. More than three-quarters of the billion-dollar fires have occurred since 2016, including the $36.3 billion Palisades fire in Los Angeles in 2025 and the $6 billion Lahaina fire in Hawaii in 2023.
Burned cars and homes in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire in Lahaina, Hawaii on 2023. Photographer: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
Climate change is contributing to conditions that increase the likelihood that fires ignite and spread, Smith said. At the same time, increasingly valuable real estate and rising reconstruction costs in areas where communities meet wildlands mean there is more to lose when fires occur.
California dominates the tally, accounting for 23 of the 31 billion-dollar fires and $167 billion of the losses. The others struck in Hawaii, Colorado, Oregon, New Mexico, Tennessee, Texas and Washington.
The analysis changes the way the economic toll of wildfires is measured, looking at fires separately instead of combining all the fires during one season into a single collective disaster. The change produces a more detailed picture but also a lower overall price tag. Under the previous approach, wildfire losses totaled $221 billion, compared with about $186 billion using the new one. The older method included losses from many smaller fires that don’t individually meet the $1 billion threshold.
For decades, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) maintained the US Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters database, tracking the nation’s most expensive hurricanes, floods, droughts, wildfires and other events.
NOAA discontinued the project in 2025. Climate Central began operating the database that October, with Smith, who had spent 15 years as lead scientist for the NOAA project, continuing to helm the research.
Climate Central’s goal was to continue the federal dataset, Smith said, expanding the detail available on wildfires while retaining the methodology for assessing other types of disasters. Next year, the group plans to go further, identifying individual fires that caused at least $100 million in damage going back to 1980.
Including the newly separated wildfire events, Climate Central counts 453 billion-dollar US weather and climate disasters since 1980, with total losses of $3.2 trillion.

Property insurers are prohibited from canceling or declining to renew coverage for 50,000 residential policyholders in Tuolumne, Stanislaus and Calaveras counties for one year following the Dove Fire.
California Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara issued the moratorium following Gov. Gavin Newsom’s Oct. 15 emergency declaration. The moratorium applies to properties in 15 ZIP codes within or around the fire perimeter, regardless of whether they suffered losses.
The moratorium also extends to certain commercial property policies, including coverage for homeowners associations, apartment complexes, condominium associations, student housing and senior living facilities.
Insurers that issued cancellation or nonrenewal notices due to wildfire risk on or after the emergency declaration must offer to rescind those notices and reinstate or renew eligible policies.
Wildfire moratoriums protected more than 1.2 million homeowners in 2025 and more than 4 million statewide since the residential moratorium law was enacted in 2019, according to the California Department of Insurance.

The driver of a minivan that crashed outside a Los Angeles metro station, killing three women and critically injuring two more, was arrested on suspicion of driving under the influence and three counts of murder, police said.
Authorities said the driver was able to talk but appeared to be in shock after Tuesday’s crash, which hit pedestrians and food vendors at a busy intersection in the North Hollywood neighborhood during the height of the evening commute.
Police identified the driver as Ihor Demianenko, 61, who lives in the Valley Village neighborhood. Demianenko was booked early Wednesday and his bail was set at a little over $6 million, records show. He was treated for minor injuries at a hospital, police said.
It wasn’t immediately clear if Demianenko had a lawyer who might speak on his behalf. In California, drivers under the influence of drugs or alcohol can be charged with murder under certain circumstances.
The case had not been presented to the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office as of Wednesday afternoon, spokesperson Venusse Dunn said in an email.
The white Toyota Sienna was traveling at an “unsafe speed” at around 6 p.m. when it veered to the right, ran off the road and collided with a light, Los Angeles police said in a news release Wednesday. It came to rest under a food vendor’s tent.
The force of the collision threw victims in different directions, according to the news release. The driver was trapped in the vehicle until rescuers arrived.
Luis Luna-Guzman was working at a nearby burger stand when he heard a loud boom and saw people on the ground along with food and cups. People started running toward the crash.
Luna-Guzman said he found an injured woman lying near some bike racks, her face, arms and legs bloody. Her eyes were closed as she moaned in pain.
“I told her, ‘Don’t move, help is coming,'” Luna-Guzman said, adding that he saw a woman’s body nearby, while another woman was lying unmoving on the stairs leading to the station.
The three women who died were between the ages of 40 and 60, according to the police news release. Authorities haven’t released their names. The two injured women are in their 50s.
The minivan was still on the sidewalk Tuesday night under the food vendor’s tent, its driver’s-side door open and an air bag deployed. Fire engines and emergency crews worked nearby as a helicopter flew overhead.
Investigators will go through video of the crash frame by frame, Police Chief Jim McDonnell said.
“It will be probably a prolonged but a very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here,” he said.
The California Supreme Court ruled in 1981 that drivers who kill someone with a vehicle can be charged with second-degree murder if they are found to have acted with “wantonness and a conscious disregard for life” that could support a finding of implied malice. The court upheld a prosecutor’s decision to file murder charges against a driver who was determined to be legally intoxicated at the time of a fatal crash and drove at high speeds, ran a red light and had a near miss right before.
Thanawala reported from Atlanta.
